Spotted sardinella (Amblygaster sirm) is a commercially important clupeid found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, and recent field studies have provided detailed life-history parameters for this species. At the onset of independent life, the prolarvae emerge from their transparent, pelagic eggs after a relatively brief incubation period; under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], hatching occurs just 3 days [ab = 3 days] after fertilisation, a rapid developmental pace that is typical of warm-water clupeiforms. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still relying entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves, measures approximately 2 to 3 millimeters in total length and possesses a wet weight at birth estimated at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a value derived from volumetric calculations based on an egg diameter ranging from 1 to 4 millimeters. This minuscule initial mass, characteristic of pelagic spawners producing numerous small eggs, highlights the extreme vulnerability of the early larval stages. The duration of the endotrophic phase is short, as the mouth-closed larva rapidly exhausts its yolk supply and initiates the critical transition to exogenous feeding within the first several days post-hatching.

Juvenile and adult growth patterns in Amblygaster sirm have been characterised through extensive length-frequency analyses and otolith increment counts conducted across multiple populations. The species attains a maximum recorded total length of 27 centimeters [Li = 27 centimeters], representing the ultimate size that individuals can achieve under favourable environmental conditions. This asymptotic length is somewhat smaller than that of some larger congeneric species but is consistent with the moderate body size typical of many inshore clupeids. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult has been estimated at 196 grams [Wwi = 196 grams], derived from a length-weight relationship that closely fits the general allometric equation for the family Clupeidae. Field records indicate that the largest individuals are typically females, which may exhibit slightly higher condition factors than males of comparable length. The species' growth trajectory is relatively rapid during the first year of life, with the majority of somatic development occurring prior to the onset of reproductive activity.

Reproductive biology in Spotted sardinella is characterised by a relatively early onset of breeding and a moderately high fecundity, traits that are typical of small pelagic fishes subject to fluctuating recruitment. Under stable thermal conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the first spawning event occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], when individuals have completed their first year of life. At this point, the fish have reached a total length at puberty of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], representing a size threshold that correlates strongly with the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis. The synchrony between length and reproductive maturation is ecologically significant, as it ensures that individuals have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the energetic demands of gamete production and spawning migrations. Populations in lower latitudes, where water temperatures remain consistently high, may exhibit slightly earlier maturation, but the 15-centimeter benchmark appears to be a robust indicator across most of the species' range.

Fecundity and spawning frequency in Amblygaster sirm have been quantified through histological analysis of ovarian tissue and daily egg production studies. Spawning occurs in multiple batches over an extended reproductive season, with individual females producing several clutches per year. The average clutch size is approximately 1,092 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,092 eggs per spawning event], a value that scales positively with female body length. When combined with a typical spawning frequency of about one event every three days [F_R_i = about one event every three days] during the peak breeding season, this yields a substantial reproductive output. Under the typical thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the highest sustained reproductive output observed in reproductively active females corresponds to approximately 364 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 364 eggs per day], representing the daily reproduction rate. These values place Amblygaster sirm among the more fecund members of the Clupeidae, consistent with its role as a small, fast-growing planktivore that relies on high reproductive effort to compensate for significant larval and juvenile mortality in the pelagic environment.

Longevity and late-life physiology have been assessed through mark-recapture studies and the examination of otolith microstructures in older individuals. The maximum recorded lifespan for Spotted sardinella is 8 years [am = 8 years], a duration that is moderate for a clupeid of its body size but notably longer than that of many small tropical anchovies and herrings at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This figure was documented in a population subject to relatively low fishing pressure and stable environmental conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], though individuals in cooler, higher-latitude waters may achieve slightly greater ages due to reduced metabolic rates. Senescence in this species is marked by a gradual decline in body condition and reproductive output rather than a sharp post-spawning mortality event; most wild individuals succumb to natural mortality before reaching the full 8-year potential. The relatively extended lifespan, combined with early maturation and high fecundity, positions Amblgaster sirm as an iteroparous species capable of multiple reproductive seasons, a life history strategy that buffers against years of poor recruitment.
